title: All things new (Apocalypse 21:1–5)
hookLine: God shall wipe away every tear
carry: behold, I make all things new

lines: A SCRAPED KNEE ON THE SIDEWALK.
A THUMB ACROSS A WET CHEEK.
cards: A kid falls off a bike. Scraped knee, gravel in the palm, a howl you can hear three houses away.
A parent comes running and, before the bandage, before anything, takes the child's face in both hands and wipes the tears off with a thumb. You have to be very close to do it.
Near the end of the Apocalypse, after the dragon and the beasts and Babylon, John says God will do exactly that.

teach.h: A NEW HEAVEN AND A NEW EARTH.
teach.b: Chapter twenty-one opens, in the Douay-Rheims: "And I saw a new heaven and a new earth." And the sea is no more. Some readers hear the sea as a picture of chaos, and John, remember, was on an island, cut off by water.
Then: "And I John saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband." Notice the direction.

teach.h: GOD PITCHES HIS TENT WITH US.
teach.b: The story doesn't end with people escaping earth; it ends with heaven coming to earth. A great voice says: "Behold the tabernacle of God with men, and he will dwell with them."
The Greek word behind tabernacle means a tent: God pitching his tent among his people, the same image John's Gospel uses when the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.
Catholics also call the place in church where the Eucharist is kept the tabernacle.

teach.h: NOT ALL NEW THINGS: ALL THINGS NEW.
teach.b: Then: "And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes: and death shall be no more, nor mourning, nor crying, nor sorrow shall be any more, for the former things are passed away."

teach.h: GOD SHALL WIPE AWAY ALL TEARS.
teach.b: Not prevent the tears: wipe them. They were real. Then the one on the throne speaks: "Behold, I make all things new."
Not all new things, a replacement world with the old one thrown out. All things, made new. The Catechism teaches that the universe itself will be renewed, not discarded.
The Church offers this among the readings at funerals, to families whose tears haven't been wiped yet.

how: Apocalypse 21 is among the readings families may choose for a Catholic funeral Mass, and the Church teaches that at the end of time the whole universe will be renewed, with God dwelling among his people.

a stone temple built to stand forever

games.q: all things new — tap the pairs.

s: the Apocalypse ends with people escaping earth to go up to heaven
the holy city comes down out of heaven. God comes to dwell with his people.
the line is 'I make all new things'
it's 'I make all things new': this world renewed, not thrown away.
Apocalypse 21 is one of the readings offered at Catholic funerals
families hear the promise: God shall wipe away all tears.

games.q: you're John, watching the last visions. after the dragon, the beasts and the fall of Babylon, where does the holy city go?
o: it stays far off in heaven.
it comes down out of heaven to earth.
games.why: the new Jerusalem comes down, prepared as a bride. behold the tabernacle of God with men, and he will dwell with them.

practice: Bring to mind someone who is crying right now, or sad a long time, and picture yourself kneeling close beside them, gently wiping their face.

If there's a sorrow of your own, let someone do the same for you; you can even touch your own cheek with your thumb. If you pray, rest in the promise, God shall wipe away all tears; if not, just let the gentleness stay.

wordCard.voice: Tabernacle, a tent. Apocalypse twenty-one: God pitching his tent among his people, in the new Jerusalem come down to earth. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: I make all things new (Apocalypse 21:5). kainos means new in kind, fresh.

carryVoice: Your line: behold, I make all things new. And that's week ninety: they rest not, worthy is the lamb, every tongue, clothed with the sun, what doesn't last, called to the supper, and all things new. Ninety weeks in.
